size.note: Wikipedia gives 13–15 cm and calls the bird quite bulky.

habitat: Forages on aerial insects anywhere it is regular, often over humid country and beside sandy banks. Nests in holes made by bee-eaters, kingfishers, martins and similar birds, and sometimes digs its own tunnel.
summary: A bulky blackish swift with a white chin patch, a white rump and a medium forked tail. The flight is fluttering, like Little Swift. Little Swift has a square tail and a more extensive white rump. White-rumped Swift has a deeper fork and a narrower white band. The call is a buzzing peeeeooo. SABAP1 treats it as largely resident in the low-lying northeast, south to the northeastern Transvaal.

similar.note: White-rumped Swift is slimmer, with a deeper fork and a thinner white rump crescent.
Little Swift has a square tail and a white rump that extends further onto the sides.

sources.title: The Atlas of Southern African Birds, Vol. 1 (Horus Swift)

upperparts.pattern: White rump, broader than the White-rumped Swift’s crescent and less extensive than the Little Swift’s wrap-around patch.

viewNotes.note: Blackish from below, with a white chin. The white rump shows as a rear patch.
White rump on an otherwise black upper side. The tail fork is shallower than a White-rumped Swift’s.
Bulky, with a fluttering flight and a white rump.
Swifts cling to a vertical surface. They do not settle on the ground, and a normal perched view is not described. The white chin is the front mark at a bank nest.
The white rump is the rear mark. Birds cling inside bee-eater and kingfisher tunnels.

calls.description: A buzzing peeeeooo, peeeeooo. The texts do not separate the sexes. The highest playable grade is B, from Senegal, and the filename says the file was edited by the recordist. It was not edited again here. An unedited South African flight call is only grade C.

research.note: Status is resident and all twelve months are listed. SABAP1 says it is largely resident in low-lying country south to the northeastern Transvaal, and a summer visitor only in cooler, higher areas. Wikipedia says South African birds are migratory, which conflicts with that lowland statement, so the Kruger months follow SABAP1. Chick down is not described. The call is grade B from Senegal and the file name says it was already edited.
